rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid missing late compounds. This should show whether any peaks are unretained or still retained into the hold, giving a good basis for narrowing the window and adjusting slope next.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the goal is to cut time while keeping every peak inside the gradient. The estimated elution window from the first run is roughly phi 0.18 to 0.68, so a narrower, shorter gradient centered on that range should speed the run substantially without risking truncation.

Since resolution is still far above the threshold, push for a faster fully resolved method by shortening the gradient and increasing temperature one step. This tests how much time can be removed before the closest pair begins to approach the 1.5 limit.

We have reached the maximum CRF, so now probe whether the method can be made even faster while staying at 1.000. The current worst pair still has a large margin, so reducing tG by one step is the cleanest next test.

The 6 min run still has comfortable resolution margin and a sub-8 min last peak, so shorten the gradient again to find the fastest method that remains fully resolved. This directly tests the edge before a critical pair drops below R = 1.5.

The current limiting pair is still above the 1.5 threshold, so one more reduction in tG can locate the shortest still-perfect method. If resolution breaks here, we can back off knowing 4 min is near-optimal.

At 4 min the only pair near the limit is the first two peaks, so lower phi0 one step to give the earliest region more gradient space without lengthening the run. This may improve the 1,2 separation while keeping the method at the 4 min speed that already gives CRF 1.000.

Lowering phi0 helped the first pair at 4 min, so now retest the 2 min gradient with the more favorable starting composition. This checks whether the shortest run can be rescued to full resolution by expanding the early elution region.

The 2 min gradient is too steep, and the limiting pair appears temperature-sensitive, so keep the successful 4 min slope and lower T one step to see if pair 1,2 gains extra selectivity. This may identify a more robust fast method and clarify whether temperature is the main lever for the critical pair.

Lowering temperature substantially improved the critical first pair at 4 min, so retest the 2 min gradient at 45 C to see whether the shortest method can now cross the R = 1.5 threshold. This is the most direct path to finding a faster 1.000 method than the current 4 min run.

The critical 1,2 pair improved notably when temperature dropped from 50 to 45 C, so continue that trend at the same 2 min gradient. If pair 1,2 reaches R at least 1.5 here, this will deliver the shortest fully resolved method tested so far.

The first pair keeps improving as temperature is lowered, while the run remains comfortably under 10 minutes, so test 35 C at the same 2 min gradient. This is the best chance to reach full resolution with the shortest possible gradient.

Now that 2 min at 35 C is fully resolved, trim the high-organic end slightly to see if the gradient window can be tightened without losing the last peak or hurting resolution. This could reveal whether the current phi1 is wider than necessary while preserving the shortest successful gradient time.

Lowering phi1 made the run slower, so instead test a higher phi0 to see whether the early pair can still stay resolved while pulling the whole separation earlier. This explores whether the 2 min, 35 C method can be made faster by trimming the low-organic end rather than the high end.

The higher starting organic improved speed without harming the critical first pair, so step phi0 up once more to see if the 2 min method can be pushed earlier still. This is a direct optimization of the current best short-gradient region while staying safely above the resolution threshold.

The first pair is now more comfortably resolved and the run is slightly faster, so increase phi0 one more step to test the practical upper limit before peaks become too close to unretained. This may uncover an even tighter 2 min method with all peaks still resolved and eluting very early.

The earliest peak is still retained enough at phi0 0.25, and resolution remains safely above threshold, so test phi0 0.30 to see if the method can be pushed further without creating an effectively unretained first peak. This is the next logical boundary check around the current fastest successful condition.

Phi0 0.30 is slightly too aggressive for the first pair, so step back to the successful phi0 0.25 and raise phi1 one step to see whether the broader window improves margin without materially slowing the run. This tests robustness around the current shortest fully resolved condition.

Raising phi1 to 0.70 kept full resolution and cut the last peak markedly, so test one more step higher to see if the hold region can be avoided even more effectively without collapsing the first pair. This is a focused speed optimization around the current best short method.

The 2 min method continues to speed up as phi1 increases, and the limiting pair still has a small but adequate margin, so test phi1 0.80 to find the fastest fully resolved version. This is a natural boundary search from the current best-performing region.

At phi1 0.80 the first pair is exactly on the resolution limit, so lower phi0 one step to regain a little selectivity while keeping the very fast late elution from the higher phi1. This tests whether a slightly wider window can make the method more robust without sacrificing much speed.

The best current fast method is right at the resolution threshold, so one more step higher in phi1 will define whether 0.80 is truly the upper limit or if an even faster fully resolved run exists. This is a boundary test around the apparent optimum.

Higher phi1 is too aggressive at 35 C, but the critical first pair improved as temperature decreased earlier, so combine the near-fastest window with 30 C to see if selectivity can be recovered while keeping a very short run. This targets a possible faster fully resolved method than the current phi0 0.25, phi1 0.80, 35 C condition.

Lowering temperature to 30 C restored strong resolution at a high-organic, very fast window, so now test phi1 0.85 to see whether the run can be shortened further while keeping pair 1,2 above 1.5. This is the most promising remaining edge test for a faster perfect method.

The current method is fully resolved with comfortable margin and very short t_last, so use the final injection to test whether raising phi0 one last step can trim the run further without dropping pair 1,2 below 1.5. This is the remaining boundary check most likely to beat the current fastest perfect condition.
